raw_text: (read to the end) As you may have heard, I have a Ph.D. 🤣 My Ph.D. (in Biomedical Engineering) gave me very valuable research experience and learned a lot about being a good researcher and managing research collaborations, skillsets that are serving me well at my startup @SophontAI. I am glad I got the opportunity to work on impactful research problems during my Ph.D. (applying AI to new microscopy technologies to improve cancer diagnostics and treatment decisions). I was working on generative AI in my PhD, earlier than 99.9% of people here even knew what it was. I put a lot of blood, sweat, and tears into my research, with many hardships along the way. I try (with limited success unfortunately) to use Twitter as a professional platform, which is why I have Ph.D. in my name. If you ask Grok, even it agrees that there's nothing wrong with saying Ph.D. in your account name especially in a professional setting. I do agree that in general it's stupid to overly focus on it, but it's not like I make anyone irl call me Dr. Tanishq or anything. Of course I don't deny there are tons of frauds who have PhDs and academia has its issues. But that doesn't mean a PhD is completely useless for everyone or has no signal, especially in highly technical fields. I don't even think everyone should do a Ph.D. For me it made sense since it allowed me to more easily do research in an interdisciplinary environment while getting solid mentorship. PhDs are often really good opportunities to progress in life sciences careers (although good alternatives are starting to arise now). However, if you're doing pure AI, a PhD may not always be a good investment of your time, and worthwhile AI research can be done in a variety of ways outside of a PhD program. At my startup we hire both PhDs and non-PhDs as researchers, and our non-PhDs are making tremendous contributions to our company! Many of the best researchers that I respect a lot never did a PhD. If you want to hate me simply for the fact that I worked hard to get a PhD and I indicate that on a profile I mostly use for professional purposes, so be it! I am proud of the hard work I put into it and I will not be ashamed of it :)

raw_text: Agree with Theo that the definition is the hard part. Mine is practical and human-based: An AI system that can replace an average knowledge worker. Why this definition? Because who cares about some esoteric, 13-page definition that very few people will read or understand? What we care about (mostly) is job replacement, so that's what we should use as the metric. So I think we might already have it in a fuzzy type of way, starting in like December of 2025. But I expect a product (or products) to come out in H2 of 2026, or in 2027 that is literally a worker replacement product. It onboards into your company, it watches Slack, it takes work from the boss, it does the work, it interacts with co-workers, it codes or writes reports, or sends emails...whatever the task is. This will be a hack. It won't be a true learning system, which is what the academics are waiting for. This will be like a Claude/Opus 6.x level product that basically has tons of skills and is able to make new ones after absorbing context and instruction. So basically great at "learning", but through a decent memory system, not actual updates to the weights. Again, this isn't "technical" AGI because it doesn't learn (in the model). But that's the problem with that definition: I think it's watching the wrong thing. If one or more of these products launch, that companies actually start onboarding, and they are doing real work, similar to their human employees, and it doesn't get pulled out en masse like 3 months later, then it happened. That's AGI, for all intents and purposes. Because an average workday is constant churn, switch-ups, changes, scope updates, moving goalposts, etc. And if this AI Employee product can do a *decent* job at that, while at the same time also being a super-genius in so many other ways, then it will likely be way better than the median knowledge worker. Don't think super-coder. Don't think top performer. Remember, there is ~ $10 trillion paid in knowledge work salaries per year. A vast number of those people are sending a few emails and writing a few reports per day. And making like $30 - $70K or something. With the cost of inference falling due to advancements, custom inference chips, and local model improvements, this level of decent employee will likely be a fraction of that cost in tokens / compute. And it can work 24/7 of course, and will actually follow an SOP. This is what I consider AGI. Practically.
